lesson.title: One Bad Meal: Taste Aversion and Biological Preparedness
lesson.summary: Taste aversion is a powerful form of classical conditioning in which a single pairing of a food's taste with illness can produce a lasting dislike of that taste, even when the illness follows hours later.
lesson.body:
Most classical conditioning follows a fairly strict set of rules: the neutral stimulus and unconditioned stimulus need to occur close together in time, and the pairing usually needs to happen several times before a conditioned response takes hold. Taste aversion breaks both of those rules, and the fact that it breaks them so consistently is exactly why psychologists find it so interesting.

The key research here comes from John Garcia and his colleagues, working with rats. In one well known line of experiments, rats drank flavored water and were then made nauseated, in some versions of the research through radiation exposure, well after they had already finished drinking. Despite the long delay between the taste and the sickness, often a matter of hours, the rats developed a strong aversion to that flavor after just one pairing. This stands in sharp contrast to the many repeated, closely timed pairings that ordinary classical conditioning, like Pavlov's work with tones and food, typically requires.

Garcia and his colleague Robert Koelling also showed something else important: not all pairings are equally easy to learn, a phenomenon sometimes called biological preparedness or selective association. In their research, rats readily learned to associate taste with later illness, but had a much harder time learning to associate taste with an immediate shock. Meanwhile, audiovisual cues, like a light or a sound, were readily associated with shock but not easily associated with illness. In other words, which stimulus gets linked to which consequence is not arbitrary. Animals appear biologically primed to connect taste specifically with sickness, almost certainly because that pairing has been life or death relevant across evolutionary history: an animal that eats something that later makes it sick badly needs to avoid that food in the future, even if the sickness was not immediate.

Taste and smell are closely intertwined in how flavor is actually perceived, since much of what people experience as taste is really the combined product of the tongue and the nose working together through olfaction. This is part of why taste aversions often generalize to related smells as well, and why the effect is sometimes described as a food or flavor aversion rather than a taste aversion in the narrowest sense. The practical result is familiar to almost everyone: a single bout of food poisoning after eating a particular dish can produce a lasting aversion to that food, sometimes for years, even once a person consciously knows the dish itself was probably not really to blame.
